abstract: Abstract Heterogeneous integration of Gallium Nitride (GaN) high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) via micro-transfer printing (μTP) offers a scalable route to address critical thermal management and integration challenges for high-power and high-frequency applications. However, traditional polymer adhesives used in the printing process create a thermal bottleneck due to their low thermal conductivity. This work introduces a room-temperature, heatless soldering mechanism at the device level utilizing undercooled liquid metallic core–shell (ULMCS) particles. Synthesized via the shearing liquids into complex particles (SLICE) method, these Field’s metal (Bi/In/Sn) particles are encapsulated in a self-limiting 10 nm oxide shell, maintaining a metastable liquid state until mechanical rupture triggers spontaneous solidification. To test this, GaN/AlGaN coupons were released from Qromis Substrate Technology wafers and printed onto silicon substrates using ULCMS particles. Printing parameters, including shear speed and shear distance, were optimized to ensure consistent adhesion. While initial μTP using compliant polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamps achieved high transfer yields, cross-sectional analysis revealed incomplete coalescence due to insufficient pressure applied by the stamp. To resolve this, a dual-stage integration framework was developed, incorporating a secondary rigid glass stamping step. This process successfully created a dense, metallic adhesion layer, providing a robust and cost-effective pathway for the integration of GaN devices for thermal management applications.

summary.how: GaN/AlGaN coupons from Qromis wafers printed onto silicon; shear speed and distance optimized; a dual-stage process adds a rigid glass stamping step to get a dense metallic layer.
summary.impact: Relevant to the GaN/AlGaN HEMT project as industry context on thermal interfaces in heterogeneous GaN integration; the interface layer is a candidate boundary resistance in device-scale models. Moderate relevance.
summary.what: Heatless, room-temperature metal bonding for micro-transfer printed GaN HEMTs using undercooled liquid metallic core-shell Field's metal particles.
summary.why: Polymer adhesives in micro-transfer printing create a thermal bottleneck due to low thermal conductivity.

title: Undercooled Liquid Metallic Core–Shell Particles Enabling Heatless Metal–Semiconductor Bonding for Micro-Transfer Printed GaN

abstract: Thermal and structural characterizations of hybrid bonding structures are essential for understanding heat transport in three-dimensional integrated circuits (3D-ICs). In this work, we investigate the effective thermal conductivity of the Cu/dielectric HB layer using time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) combined with picosecond ultrasonic technique. Shallow-angle polishing enabled depth-resolved thermal measurements by exposing hybrid bonding layers with different remaining thicknesses, while acoustic echoes were used to identify buried interfaces and determine the thickness. The distinct waveform of the bonding interface echo compared with the Cu/dielectric interface echo suggests that its acoustic response may also reflect the interfacial bonding conditions. The extracted thermal conductivity ranges from 1.14 to 1.75 Wm-1K-1 for the bottom pad layer and from 1.76 to 4.34 Wm-1K-1 for the top pad layer. The difference in thermal conductivity is consistent with the different Cu area fractions of the two layers. Furthermore, the thermal conductivity of the top pad layer increases significantly with the remaining thickness, possibly due to the thermal boundary resistance at the bonding interface, low thermal conductivity of SiCN interlayer, and increased electron scattering in thin Cu structures. Our work demonstrates a practical approach to investigate the thermal properties of buried hybrid bonding layers, providing experimental data for thermal design and modeling of 3D-ICs.

summary.how: Depth-resolved TDTR plus acoustic echoes to locate buried interfaces and thickness. Thermal conductivity is 1.14–1.75 W m-1K-1 for the bottom pad layer and 1.76–4.34 W m-1K-1 for the top pad layer; it depends on Cu area fraction and increases with remaining thickness.
summary.impact: Moderate relevance to electronics thermal-management industry trends: it provides experimental effective-κ and boundary-resistance data for 3D-IC packaging that device-scale thermal simulations (e.g., JAX-BTE, interface models) could use as input or benchmarks.
summary.what: Measured the effective thermal conductivity of Cu/dielectric hybrid bonding layers in 3D-ICs with TDTR combined with picosecond ultrasonics and shallow-angle polishing.
summary.why: Heat transport in hybrid bonding structures must be understood for thermal design of 3D-ICs.

title: Thermal and Acoustic Measurements of Hybrid Bonding Stacks

abstract: VQkit is a Python-based computational toolkit developed to streamline the pre- and post-processing of density functional theory calculations performed using Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) and Quantum ESPRESSO (QE). The framework employs a unified representation of lattice vectors, atomic coordinates, chemical species, and positional constraints, enabling cross-code structure conversion, geometry manipulation, crystallographic reconstruction, and code-specific input generation. Its pre-processing capabilities include symmetry-dependent reciprocal-space path generation, atomic constraints, and automated preparation of simulation inputs. The post-processing framework provides calculation convergence inspection, extraction of total energies and Fermi levels, electronic band-structure and density-of-states analysis, orbital-resolved electronic-structure processing, charge-density analysis, and evaluation of application-specific materials properties. The computational implementation is evaluated through elastic-property benchmarks for HfC, ZrC, ZrO2, Ti, and diamond, showing close agreement between VQkit and VASPKIT for VASP-based calculations, with differences observed in the corresponding QE results. By integrating cross-code interoperability, automated simulation preparation, standardized post-processing, and quantitative property evaluation within a common computational environment, VQkit reduces workflow fragmentation and facilitates consistent pre- and post-processing of first-principles calculations.

summary.how: Unified structure representation; benchmarked on elastic properties of HfC, ZrC, ZrO2, Ti and diamond, agreeing closely with VASPKIT for VASP, with differences in the QE results.
summary.impact: Possibly useful: you use VASP, so it could streamline structure and input handling for the lattice-dynamics and MLIP training-data pipelines. Not a phonon-specific tool; it is worth a quick look rather than an adoption decision.
summary.what: Presents VQkit, a Python toolkit for pre- and post-processing DFT calculations in VASP and Quantum ESPRESSO, with cross-code structure conversion and input generation.
summary.why: Fragmented pre- and post-processing across DFT codes makes workflows inconsistent.

title: VQkit: A Unified and Extensible Framework for VASP and Quantum ESPRESSO Pre- and Post-Processing

abstract: Tensor-product (TP) layers in equivariant interatomic potentials encode angular interactions through symmetry-allowed paths. Yet local site symmetry can make an allowed path carry no signal after neighbor aggregation. We call this effect Aggregation Cancellation. In a scalar-input first layer, equal-species neighbors on a complete site-symmetry orbit share scalar and radial factors, reducing their angular contribution to a spherical-harmonic orbit sum. If the restricted degree-l representation has no trivial component, this sum and the corresponding path vanish for any learned radial weight. For an ideal Oₕ octahedral orbit, this removes the lₑdge=1,2,3 classes. Beyond the first layer, the factorisation no longer holds, so cancellation is no longer guaranteed; we instead ask whether affected paths remain less important on average. We test the two levels separately in NequIP: matched-radius TiO₆ probes examine first-layer cancellation, whereas a within-model CaTiO₃ comparison and six OMat24 models examine the importance bias. We then rank paths on training frames, choose the pruning fraction on validation frames, and evaluate frozen masks on held-out tests. At the highest evaluated fraction (60% of 174 paths), force mean absolute error (MAE) changes are 1.42%, 0.04%, and 1.83% for CaTiO₃, OMat24 Oₕ-cubic, and OMat24 low-symmetry data, respectively. The masks imply 67.12-71.94% potential TP-operation reduction and 59.77% potential edge multilayer perceptron (MLP) reduction; these are structural proxies, not measured speedups. The results connect local symmetry to path redundancy and pruning robustness in NequIP; transfer to other architectures remains open.

summary.how: Probes on TiO₆, CaTiO₃ and six OMat24 models; pruning 60% of 174 paths changed force MAE by 1.42%, 0.04% and 1.83% on CaTiO₃, OMat24 Oₕ-cubic and low-symmetry data. Speedups are structural proxies only, not measured.
summary.impact: Relevant to the MLIP interpretability and efficiency interest: the symmetry-based analysis of equivariant models (MACE-like) could inform path pruning for faster MLIPs in the perovskite oxide (BaTiO₃, SrTiO₃) work. Transfer to other architectures is stated as open.
summary.what: Group-theoretic analysis of why some tensor-product paths in equivariant MLIPs such as NequIP carry no signal (Aggregation Cancellation), plus path pruning tests.
summary.why: Local site symmetry can make symmetry-allowed paths vanish after neighbor aggregation, which suggests redundancy in equivariant models.

title: When Do Tensor Product Paths Matter? A Group-Theoretic Analysis of Equivariant Interatomic Potentials

abstract: ABSTRACT The traditional lone‐pair electron strategy primarily reduces lattice thermal conductivity ( κ L ) by enhancing anharmonic lattice vibrations. However, this mechanism has long been considered to exist only in specific cations with ns 2 electron configurations (e.g. Sb 3+ , Bi 3+ ), severely restricting the broader applicability of this lone‐pair‐based approach. In this study, CuInSnSe 4 is successfully synthesized via atomic cross‐substitution from the diamondoid CuInSe 2 , wherein the Se atoms exhibit an anionic lone‐pair‐like electronic behavior, revealing a new approach to reducing κ L that differs from conventional cation‐based mechanisms. In contrast to the traditional mechanism that relies on cations to enhance lattice anharmonicity, the anionic lone‐pair electrons weaken the Se‐Se interactions, flatten the optical phonon branches, and consequently significantly expand the scattering phase space, providing more scattering channels for phonons. This anionic lone‐pair electron strategy reduces the room‐temperature κ L from 4.48 to 1.26 W m −1 K −1 . Ultimately, the predicted optimal thermoelectric figure of merit ( ZT ) for p‐type and n‐type CuInSnSe 4 attains values of 1.99 and 0.79, respectively. This work systematically expands the conventional application boundaries of the lone‐pair electron strategy and elucidates a fundamentally distinct mechanism for κ L reduction, providing a new theoretical basis for designing and developing novel high‐efficiency thermoelectric materials with intrinsically low κ L .

summary.how: The anionic lone pairs weaken Se-Se interactions, flatten optical phonon branches and enlarge the scattering phase space.
summary.impact: Moderate relevance for mechanism understanding: phase-space and anharmonicity arguments mirror the phonon analysis in lattice-dynamics workflows (ALAMODE, phono3py), though the material is a thermoelectric chalcogenide.
summary.what: CuInSnSe4 made by atomic cross-substitution from CuInSe2: anionic lone-pair-like Se electrons cut room-temperature κL from 4.48 to 1.26 W/m·K; predicted ZT of 1.99 (p-type) and 0.79 (n-type).
summary.why: Lone-pair strategies for lowering κL were thought limited to ns2 cations such as Sb3+ and Bi3+.

title: Anionic Lone‐Pair‐Like Electrons Induced Ultra‐Low Lattice Thermal Conductivity and High Thermoelectric Performance

abstract: Abstract Eco-friendly Cu3SbSe4 is a promising mid-temperature thermoelectric material. Although Sn-doped Cu3SbSe4 optimizes thermoelectric properties, it also negatively impacts thermal properties. Herein, Cu3Sb0.98Sn0.02Se4-x%PbSe composites were synthesized via an integrated microwave-hydrothermal and spark plasma sintering route. Subsequent characterizations reveal the coexistence of a Cu3SbSe4-based matrix and PbSe secondary phases at higher PbSe contents, while the evolution of the lattice parameters suggests possible partial Pb incorporation into the matrix. The PbSe/Cu3SbSe4 heterointerfaces may contribute to energy-dependent carrier filtering, which is consistent with the enhanced Seebeck coefficient observed after PbSe formation. Concurrently, the coexistence of point defects, grain boundaries, and PbSe-rich regions provides multiple structural features that may contribute to phonon scattering and the evolution of lattice thermal conductivity. First-principles calculations also elucidate that this co-doping strategy fundamentally reconstructs the electronic band structure and phonon dispersion. Consequently, the Cu3Sb0.98Sn0.02Se4-4%PbSe composite delivers a maximum power factor of 999.35 μW m–1 K–2 and a peak zT of 0.77 at 623 K. These results demonstrate that PbSe incorporation provides an additional route for regulating the electrical and thermal transport properties of Sn-doped Cu3SbSe4.

summary.how: Microwave-hydrothermal synthesis with spark plasma sintering; heterointerfaces, point defects and grain boundaries scatter phonons; first-principles calculations of bands and phonon dispersion.
summary.impact: Low relevance; experimental thermoelectric synthesis, with only loose links to interface phonon scattering.
summary.what: Cu3Sb0.98Sn0.02Se4 with PbSe composites reaching peak zT of 0.77 at 623 K and power factor of 999.35 μW/m·K2.
summary.why: Sn doping optimizes thermoelectric properties but harms thermal properties of Cu3SbSe4.

title: Synergistic Enhancement of Thermoelectric Properties in Cu3SbSe4 via Multiscale Phonon Scattering and Energy Filtering Effects

abstract: ABSTRACT This investigation explores the structural, elastic, electronic, optical, thermal, and thermodynamic properties of silicide compounds (XAl 2 Si 2 , X = Y, La) using density functional theory (DFT). The structural stability and mechanical characteristics were evaluated through elastic constants, micro‐ and macro‐hardness, Cauchy pressure, Pugh's ratio, and Poisson's ratio. The calculated elastic parameters confirm the mechanical stability of both compounds, while the obtained Pugh's ratio, Poisson's ratio, and Cauchy pressure values indicate their ductile nature. Bond population analysis reveals the coexistence of ionic and covalent bonding characteristics. The electronic properties were investigated through band structures and density of states calculations, including spin–orbit coupling (SOC) effects to explore possible topological features. Furthermore, phonon dispersion and thermodynamic analyses were performed to evaluate dynamic and thermal stability. The combination of favorable electrical properties and moderate lattice thermal conductivity suggests potential applications in thermoelectric and high‐temperature environments. Optical investigations reveal that both compounds exhibit reflectance above 75% in the visible region, indicating their capability for reducing solar heat absorption. Additionally, their high refractive index at low photon energies and strong ultraviolet (UV) absorption behavior makes them promising candidates for optoelectronic and UV‐protection applications.

summary.how: DFT with elastic constants, band structure with SOC, phonon dispersion and thermodynamic analysis.
summary.impact: Low relevance; routine DFT property survey of materials outside the listed projects.
summary.what: DFT study of the structural, elastic, electronic, optical and thermal properties of YAl2Si2 and LaAl2Si2.
summary.why: To evaluate the mechanical stability and potential thermoelectric, optoelectronic and UV-protection applications.

title: DFT‐Based Investigation of the Mechanical, Optoelectronic, Bonding, Thermophysical, and Thermodynamic Properties of XAl 2 Si 2 (X = Y, La) Silicides for Potential Applications

abstract: Accurate first-principles characterization of excitons typically relies on the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) combined with quasiparticle energies from computationally demanding GW calculations. Here, we replace the GW step with quasiparticle energies from Koopmans-compliant spectral functionals, an approach we call BSE@qKI, and implement it in an automated, reproducible AiiDA workflow. For a set of benchmark semiconductors, BSE@qKI reproduces experimental band gaps and first exciton energies with mean absolute relative errors of 13% and 4%, respectively, comparable to BSE@G0W0 for the gaps and markedly better for the excitation energies. We also apply the method to the layered magnetic semiconductor CrI3, obtaining an absorption spectrum that reproduces the main experimental features. These results establish BSE@qKI as a GW-free alternative to BSE@G0W0 for systematic studies of excitonic properties in complex materials.

abstract: Abstract Cu2ABX4-based chalcogenides, characterized by the inherently restricted lattice thermal transport associated with low structural symmetry and complexity, have emerged as promising candidates for advanced thermoelectric (TE) applications. Herein, tetragonal Cu2CdSiTe4 is systematically investigated through an integrated methodology comprising first-principles calculations, machine-learning interatomic potentials, and Boltzmann transport theory coupled with a two-channel model. Cu2CdSiTe4 exhibits distinct structural merits, including distorted tetrahedral coordination, a spatially separated conductive Cu2Te4 unit and an insulating CdSiTe4 framework, as well as strong acoustic–optical coupling. These features synergistically induce intense phonon scattering, flattened phonon dispersions, and pronounced lattice anharmonicity, resulting in a reduced lattice thermal conductivity (κl) of 0.76 W m–1 K–1 at 700 K. Electronic structure calculations further reveal an indirect bandgap of 0.85 eV and multi-valley band characteristics, which facilitate enhanced carrier transport and electrical conductivity (σ). Under the phonon two-channel model, p-type Cu2CdSiTe4 achieves a maximum dimensionless figure-of-merit (ZT) of 1.75 at 700 K, demonstrating promising prospects for TE applications.

summary.how: DFT, MLIPs, Boltzmann transport theory and a phonon two-channel model; strong acoustic–optical coupling and anharmonicity give flattened dispersions and strong scattering.
summary.impact: Low-to-moderate relevance: the MLIP + BTE + two-channel workflow resembles the MLPhonon pipeline and could inform handling of strongly anharmonic, low-κ materials, but the material is not among the current projects.
summary.what: Studies tetragonal Cu2CdSiTe4 thermoelectrics using first-principles calculations, MLIPs and Boltzmann transport with a two-channel (phonon + diffuson) model; reports κl of 0.76 W m–1 K–1 at 700 K and ZT of 1.75 at 700 K.

title: Diffuson-Assisted Hierarchy of Thermal Transport in Anharmonic Cu2CdSiTe4 Thermoelectrics

abstract: Abstract Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become powerful tools for material simulations. Many MLIPs are trained based on density functional theory (DFT) datasets generated with the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange−correlation functional. Using a PBE-based MLIP for HfO2, we identify a low-energy I41/amd structure, which is predicted to be more stable than the well-known ground-state structure, the monoclinic P21/c structure. Since experiments show clearly that HfO2 takes the P21/c structure as the ground state, this is obviously a wrong prediction. Unfortunately, the same prediction is also made by widely used PBE-based foundation models, such as NequIP-OAM-L and MatterSim-v1-5M. Comparisons among different DFT functionals in this work show that PBE exhibits stabilization of low-density structures containing sixfold Hf−O octahedral units, such as the I41/amd and Pbcn phases, leading to incorrect energetic ordering. The error also affects the calculated energy landscapes and barrier heights along ferroelectric HfO2 polarization switching paths when there are large lattice relaxations. Fortunately, the error can be largely suppressed by other functionals such as PBEsol and local density approximation. Our study serves as a warning about the impact of errors in exchange−correlation functional approximations on the reliability of MLIP simulations of crystal structures and phase transitions.

summary.how: Compared DFT functionals: PBE over-stabilizes low-density sixfold Hf–O octahedral phases, while PBEsol and LDA largely remove the error. The error also affects ferroelectric switching barriers.
summary.impact: Useful for the MLIP failure-modes interest: a caution for MACE and Deep Potential models trained on PBE data in the InGaAs, BAs, GaN and BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃ (oxide) projects. Check the functional choice, especially for oxides and lattice-relaxation-sensitive properties.
summary.what: Shows that PBE-based MLIPs, including NequIP-OAM-L and MatterSim-v1-5M foundation models, wrongly predict an I41/amd structure of HfO2 as more stable than the experimental P21/c ground state.
summary.why: MLIPs trained on PBE data inherit functional errors, which affect the reliability of structure and phase-transition simulations.

title: A Wrong Ground-State Structure of HfO2 Predicted by Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Based on the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof Functional

abstract: Gallium nitride (GaN)-based high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs), which employ GaN as the active material, are expected to exhibit high breakdown voltages and high electron saturation velocities. Extensive research and development efforts are currently being conducted to further enhance their performance. One of the major challenges for GaN HEMTs lies in maintaining stable operation under high-temperature conditions. Therefore, further investigation into HEMT structures capable of withstanding higher breakdown voltages and offering improved thermal stability is required. To address this issue, we have focused on an N-polar GaN/AlGaN/AlN HEMT, which utilizes AlN—a material with approximately twice the bandgap energy of GaN and superior thermal conductivity—as a buffer layer. This structure is expected to provide a higher breakdown voltage and improved high-temperature performance than the conventional Ga-polar AlGaN/GaN HEMT. In this study, we evaluated the temperature-dependent characteristics of N-polar GaN/AlGaN/AlN HEMTs over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C in order to investigate the high-temperature operation. As a result, the N-polar GaN/AlGaN/AlN HEMT exhibited stable DC characteristics up to 600 °C, demonstrating superior high-temperature operation compared with the conventional AlGaN/GaN HEMT.

abstract: Cu–diamond composites are recognized as promising high-thermal-conductivity candidates for electronic cooling, offering tunable properties and competitive cost. However, their performance is significantly limited by the poor Cu/diamond interfacial thermal conductance (ITC). Here, we propose a nitrogen-termination strategy to tune the ITC of Cu/diamond interfaces and unravel atomistic mechanisms by which nitride interlayers tailor phonon transport. Based on the MACE machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) framework, we fine-tune the pre-trained MACE-MPA-0 foundation model by incorporating customized C–N–Cu training datasets. Incorporating non-equilibrium molecular dynamics with MLIP-driven lattice dynamics simulations, we demonstrate that anharmonic effects contribute ∼60% to the ITC, and simply introducing N-termination on the diamond surface enhances the ITC by 10% compared to the bare Cu/diamond interface. However, the enhancement of harmonic phonon transmission contributes ∼80% of the ITC improvement. Mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy reveals that the LA phonons with frequencies above 4 THz and wavevectors near the Γ–X and Γ–U directions are selectively modulated by N-termination engineering. Analyses of local vibrational states and interfacial bonding further indicate that the N-termination on diamond tunes the interfacial heat conduction via surficial mass modification and chemical bonding regulation, as evidenced by variations in LDOS overlaps and COHP spectra. These findings open venues for tuning heat transfer across Cu/diamond interfaces via non-metallic modification—which avoids the graphitization issues associated with metallic coatings—and provide novel guidelines for upgrading the phonon-mediated heat transfer in Cu–diamond composites.

summary.impact: Highly relevant to the GaN/Al₂O₃ interface and BAs interface work and to the MLPhonon workflow: it is a template for fine-tuning MACE and combining NEMD with lattice-dynamics ITC decomposition (harmonic vs anharmonic, mode-resolved).

summary.why: Poor Cu/diamond ITC limits Cu–diamond composites for electronic cooling, and metallic coatings cause graphitization.

title: Tuning Cu/diamond interfacial thermal conductance via nitrogen-termination engineering

abstract: Poster presented at eNergetics 2026, the 6th International Conference on Energy and Environment, 23 to 24 November 2026 (virtual). Cubic CsPbBr₃ is the phase that exists above 403 K, which is the temperature range relevant to waste-heat recovery. Almost all reported measurements, however, are made on the room-temperature orthorhombic polymorph, and while the electronic structure of the cubic phase is established, its lattice dynamics and transport properties are not. This work presents one internally consistent set of first-principles calculations for the cubic phase, covering electronic structure with spin-orbit coupling, optical response, lattice dynamics and thermoelectric transport. Quantities reported here that were not previously available for this phase include the Seebeck coefficient and the thermoelectric figure of merit, the acoustic deformation potentials of both band edges, the R-point soft-mode frequency, and the Debye temperature, sound velocity and Grüneisen parameter. ZT reaches 0.39 at 800 K near 10¹⁹ cm⁻³, with p-type and n-type values equal to within a few percent. Because the lattice thermal conductivity already sits at the Cahill-Pohl glassy minimum of 0.475 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, the ceiling on ZT is set by the power factor rather than by heat transport. Lowering the lattice thermal conductivity further therefore cannot raise ZT in this family, and only the electronic side can be improved. Methods: VASP 5.4.4 with the projector augmented-wave method, PBE and HSE06 functionals and spin-orbit coupling throughout; phonons from finite displacements in a 2x2x2 supercell using Phonopy; electronic transport from BoltzTraP2 within the constant relaxation-time approximation, with the relaxation time taken from Fröhlich polaron theory rather than fitted to experiment.…

abstract: Controlling antiferromagnetic (AFM) domains is essential for spintronics, yet predictable manipulation remains challenging due to their lack of net magnetization. Here, we utilize scanning electron microscopy electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI) to observe the formation of nanoscale AFM domains in epitaxial NiO/MgO(001) at interface dislocations. Thermal cycling across the Néel temperature reveals that while domain contrast vanishes in the paramagnetic phase, the features re-emerge at identical spatial locations upon cooling. Diffraction-vector-dependent ECCI imaging, governed by a relative tilt contrast model, indicates that the domains stem from localized rhombohedral distortions of volumetric twin-type T-domains. These T-domains are stabilized by the long-range shear stress field of interface misfit dislocations (MDs). By tracking a film thickness series from 23 to 46 nm, we resolve a transition in oxide relaxation mechanics from primary 60° interface MDs along ⟨110⟩ to a cross-slipped network of pure edge 90° MDs deviated toward ⟨100⟩. We demonstrate that ECCI identifies the Burgers vector and line direction of these MDs via strict g→·(b→×u→) invisibility criteria, and an Eshelby interaction energy model accurately predicts the asymmetric nucleation of specific T-domains along MD flanks. Quantitative image analysis shows that T-domain volume fractions track the spatial configuration of the evolving MD networks, providing a framework for defect-engineering AFM textures using one-dimensional defects.

abstract: ABSTRACT Recent advances in thermally conductive composites have significantly improved heat dissipation, yet the scalable and low‐cost fabrication of isotropic high thermal conductivity materials remains a major challenge. Here, we present a mechanochemical strategy for the stable integration of liquid metal (LM) with aluminum (Al) flakes, producing Al@LM (AlM) heterogeneous fillers. The unique Al‐Al 2 O 3 ‐LM heterostructure enables LM to form a hot carrier bridge between adjacent AlMs. The thermal resistance of LM bridge is only 1.37 × 10 −9 m 2 K/W, which is one order of magnitude lower than that of the Al 2 O 3 ‐Al 2 O 3 imperfect interface. As a result, the composites achieve an isotropic thermal conductivity of 17.59 W/m·K (surpassing that of 304 steel) while maintaining a flexural strength of 65.4 MPa. The Al 2 O 3 shell blocks electron transport yet permits phonon transfer, conferring excellent electrical insulation (1.5 × 10 9 Ω/cm). Beyond serving as bulk plastics, the composite can function as adhesive, exhibiting thermal resistance of only 13.3 mm 2 K/W and shear adhesive strength of 6.3 MPa. Meanwhile, the dynamic covalent network of matrix enables composites to maintain thermal management performance after repeated processing and recycling. This work establishes a simple and scalable strategy for stabilizing LMs on Al fillers and advancing sustainable thermal management materials.

abstract: This work presents a single-event radiation-hardened p-GaN gate high electron mobility transistor with a grounded Schottky contact (GSC-HEMT). A Schottky contact connected to the source electrode is fabricated on the barrier layer between the gate and drain terminals. Under Ta ion irradiation with a linear energy transfer of 82.06 MeV cm2/mg, the GSC-HEMT exhibits a significantly enhanced single-event burnout (SEB) voltage of over 500 V, demonstrating excellent SEB tolerance. In the conventional p-GaN HEMT, irradiation-induced holes accumulate beneath the gate region, resulting in a larger local electric field and increased gate leakage current. The proposed GSC-HEMT is capable of rapidly collecting irradiation-induced holes through its grounded Schottky contact. This structure can effectively suppress the massive accumulation of positive charges under the gate and within the buffer layer, thereby improving the radiation tolerance of the device. The designed device demonstrates great application prospects in aerospace electronics.

abstract: ABSTRACT Hexagonal boron nitride (BN), due to its high thermal conductivity (TC), excellent electrical insulation, and low dielectric constant, has become an ideal filler for designing advanced thermal management materials (TMMs), effectively addressing thermal failure and electromagnetic leakage issues in advanced chips. BN structures in different dimensions (0D, 1D, and 2D) each have their own advantages, their interface morphology directly affects the TC of composite systems. However, there is still a lack of systematic understanding of phonon transport behavior at different interfaces in composite systems and their impact on thermal conduction network construction. This review focuses on dimensional classification and compares the intrinsic TC, phonon transport mechanisms, and network formation behavior of 0D, 1D, and 2D BN fillers. In addition to the traditional filler/polymer interfaces, this analysis also focused on the phonon transport properties at the homogeneous and heterogeneous nanoadditives interfaces of BN. At the same time, the TC of mono‐, di‐, and multi‐component nanoadditives systems were systematically evaluated, revealing the synergistic effects among BN of different dimensions. This review aims to provide a reference for reducing the thermal resistance of complex interfaces and promoting the practical application of micro–nano materials in the field of thermal management.

abstract: β-Ga2O3 is a promising semiconductor due to its physical properties, such as an ultra-wide bandgap of ∼4.8 eV and an estimated critical breakdown field of 8 MV/cm, making it attractive for power devices. Nevertheless, discrepancies remain regarding the nature of the fundamental optical transition, while accurate knowledge of this parameter is crucial for technological implementation. Hence, in this study, optical transitions were investigated at room temperature for β-Ga2O3 layers grown by metalorganic chemical vapor deposition on (010)-oriented β-Ga2O3 substrates. Subsequently, the samples were studied by contactless electroreflectance (CER) and photoacoustic spectroscopy (PAS), which are sensitive to direct and indirect transitions, respectively. Moreover, the density functional theory calculations were performed to support the experimental data. The fundamental energy gap (band-to-band transition) in β-Ga2O3 was found to be indirect, with a value of 4.84 ± 0.02 eV determined by PAS, while two direct optical transitions were identified in CER at 4.86 ± 0.02 and 5.17 ± 0.02 eV. These transitions have an excitonic character, which further supports the conclusion about the indirect nature of the bandgap in this crystal. The exciton binding energy estimated from PAS and CER measurements for the fundamental excitonic transition is ∼30 meV, which is significantly less than previously reported and can be considered as a lower experimental estimate. Due to the small difference between the indirect and direct gap and the large exciton binding energy, the excitonic absorption spectrally overlaps with the indirect absorption and makes it difficult to determine the indirect energy gap in optical measurements.

abstract: Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics (MCMD) simulations are widely used to study the properties of materials at the mesoscale. Simulations with hundreds of thousands of atoms usually rely on empirical potentials because MCMD with machine-learning interatomic potentials is impractical at this scale in existing implementations. Here, we introduce a hybrid MPI/OpenMP scheme for MCMD with Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) potentials in LAMMPS. Monte Carlo moves are evaluated from local energy changes and carried out in parallel over MPI ranks, while molecular dynamics is parallelized over OpenMP threads. At a fixed number of CPUs, the wall time of the Monte Carlo moves decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks. Larger simulation cells also reduce the statistical errors of free energy calculations because thermal fluctuations decrease with system size. We demonstrate the scheme by calculating free energies of the HCP and BCC phases in the strongly anharmonic Hf--Ti system and by simulating zirconium segregation in a nanocrystalline copper sample of 670,000 atoms. For Cu--Zr, an ACE potential and an empirical potential predict similar grain boundary compositions but different amounts of zirconium dissolved in the grains. The scheme makes MCMD simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials practical at the length scales of microstructure.

abstract: Dissociative water adsorption is a key step in heterogeneous and electrochemical catalysis, but on finite Ni nanosystems the OH$^*$ and H$^*$ fragments can occupy many combinations of surface sites, making exhaustive density functional theory (DFT) screening impractical. We introduce a graph neural network (GNN) framework with an adsorbate-free representation: candidate O- and H-binding sites are defined by sets of Ni atoms (\textit{anchors}), and each site pair is encoded as a graph constructed solely from these anchors and their local Ni environment. Using only MACE-relaxed bare Ni geometries as input, separate GNNs predict the DFT-reference adsorption energies of OH$^*$+H$^*$ configurations and whether the proposed binding sites would be retained upon DFT relaxation, eliminating the need to construct or relax adsorbates during screening. Trained across Ni nanoclusters and Ni(111)/Ni(100) surfaces, the energy model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.031 eV on the internal validation set and demonstrates transferability to unseen Ni$_{55}$, Ni$_{91}$, and Ni$_{130}$ clusters and larger surface cells, particularly for relative-energy ranking, although quantitative accuracy varies across systems. These independent tests also support the retention classifier's use as a conservative filter for selecting configurations likely to preserve their proposed binding sites. Application to Ni nanoparticles containing up to $\sim$3000 atoms identifies favorable co-adsorption motifs and shows that lower O-site coordination generally stabilizes the dissociated state, whereas H-site coordination has a weaker influence. The framework thus offers an efficient route to screening adsorption energetics, with potential extensions to other metals and adsorbate combinations.

abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. abstract: In this study, we investigate the slow-wave amplification mechanism in an interdigitated-gated 2D electron gas (2DEG) and conduct design and analysis of its performance by combining a 3D full-wave model for extrinsic properties and an Finite-difference Time-domain Particle-in-cell (FDTD-PIC) model for intrinsic 2D modeling. The FDTD-PIC method is developed and applied for modeling electromagnetic (EM) wave propagation as well as 2DEG particle dynamics in a coupled manner. The modeling investigates the effect of device geometry, input and output feeding co-planar waveguide line structure, and 2DEG parameters, such as the effect of applied RF power, drift velocity, and frequency. The 2DEG dynamics reveal a velocity fluctuation of 25%, leading to effects such as electron bunching and amplification of current oscillations in the channel. abstract: We report an unusual nonmonotonic temperature dependence of the optical band gap in the layered nitride halide TiNCl, revealed by temperature-dependent photoluminescence (PL) and diffuse reflectance spectroscopy. The band gap, determined from the PL spectra, decreases with increasing temperature at low temperatures, reaches a minimum near 50 K, and then increases at higher temperatures. This behavior contrasts with the monotonic decrease typically observed in conventional semiconductors. The observed temperature dependence is well reproduced by a Bose-Einstein oscillator model with two characteristic phonon energies of approximately 8.9 meV and 1.2 meV. Based on temperature-dependent X-ray diffraction measurements and first-principles calculations using the experimental lattice parameters, we found that the contribution of thermal expansion is negligibly small compared with the observed band-gap variation. Furthermore, first-principles phonon calculations for the optimized crystal structure revealed peaks in the phonon density of states near these two characteristic energies. These results suggest that electron-phonon interactions play an important role in the anomalous temperature dependence of the optical band gap in TiNCl, with low- and higher-energy phonons contributing to the low-temperature decrease and the higher-temperature increase, respectively.

abstract: Black phosphorus is an emerging low-dimensional semiconductor whose tunable band gap, high carrier mobility, and anisotropic transport make it attractive for directional energy transport in electronics and thermoelectrics. Using ultrafast stroboscopic optical scattering microscopy (stroboSCAT), we image spatiotemporal evolution of energy carriers with picosecond resolution, simultaneously resolving heat and charge transport in bulk black phosphorus and exciton transport in the monolayer. The in-plane armchair:zigzag anisotropy increases from 5.3:1 in the bulk to 6.7:1 in the monolayer, driven by enhanced armchair exciton diffusivity (45.5 cm$^2$/s) relative to bulk armchair charge carriers (16.5 cm$^2$/s). The monolayer anisotropy is smaller than the calculated exciton dispersion alone would suggest, which first-principles calculations attribute to preferential exciton-phonon scattering to large momenta along the zigzag direction. These directly measured, layer-resolved diffusivities identify armchair-aligned monolayers as the optimal geometry for directional transport and show that transport anisotropy cannot be inferred from band dispersion alone.

summary.how: Picosecond-resolution optical scattering microscopy plus first-principles calculations attributing the result to exciton-phonon scattering to large momenta along the zigzag direction.
summary.impact: Low relevance to the listed projects; anisotropy of transport is conceptually related to phonon direction asymmetry in BaTiO3.
summary.what: Ultrafast stroboSCAT imaging of heat, charge and exciton transport in black phosphorus: armchair:zigzag anisotropy rises from 5.3:1 in bulk to 6.7:1 in the monolayer.
summary.why: To resolve directional energy transport in an anisotropic low-dimensional semiconductor.

title: Ultrafast Imaging Reveals Energy Transport Anisotropy Grows from Bulk to Monolayer Black Phosphorus

abstract: In this work, the mechanism of single-event burnout (SEB) in p-GaN gate HEMTs is thoroughly investigated by irradiation experiments and simulations. The samples were irradiated with tantalum (Ta) ions (67 MeV cm2/mg in GaN). There are two distinct failure modes observed in samples occurring in SEB. One is the four-terminal short-circuit mode, and the other is the vertical short-circuit mode between the drain and the substrate. By comparing damaged structures, it can be inferred that both failure modes probably originated from the burnout of the drain. According to the transient currents and temperature distributions by simulations, it is found that the most sensitive region to SEB is the edge of the drain, rather than the edge of the gate or field plate. The SEB mechanism can be explained as follows. A large number of generated holes accumulate at the GaN/AlN interface, while a large number of electrons will accumulate at the Si-Sub/AlN interface, leading to a high electric field in the AlN layer and in turn enhancing the impact ionization. Then the generated electrons will drift to the drain and concentrate around the drain, which produces high current density as well as a high electric field near the drain. Therefore, the lattice temperature there is quickly raised to trigger thermal runaway at the drain.

summary.how: Irradiation experiments, damage comparison, and simulated transient currents and temperature distributions; hole accumulation at GaN/AlN and electron accumulation at Si/AlN interfaces enhance impact ionization and lead to thermal runaway at the drain.
summary.impact: Some relevance to the GaN HEMT project, since lattice temperature rise and thermal runaway at the drain are device self-heating effects, although this is a radiation study. Low to moderate.
summary.what: Investigates single-event burnout in p-GaN gate HEMTs through Ta ion irradiation (67 MeV cm2/mg) and simulation, finding two failure modes and the drain edge as the most sensitive region.
summary.why: To explain the SEB mechanism in GaN power devices.

title: Investigation of single-event burnout mechanism in p-GaN gate HEMTs

abstract: Energy landscape exploration requires extensive energy and force evaluations, making efficient access to interatomic potentials an important practical challenge. We present a persistent socket interface that connects the landscape exploration tools in the GMIN, OPTIM, and PATHSAMPLE programs to potentials available through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). The persistent design keeps both the calculator and socket connection active throughout the search, avoiding repeated initialisation. We apply this framework to understand and predict the properties of Ga vacancies in $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ using two NequIP-based potentials, and construct kinetic transition networks describing complex vacancy configurations and migration pathways. Temperature-dependent analysis of the dominant paths reveals how the most probable migration sequence can change, with the mechanism governed by global properties of the network, rather than simply the highest energy barrier. Visualisation, mean first-passage times, and heat capacities enable us to connect the organisation of the landscape to relaxation time scales and thermodynamic observables. The interface extends energy landscape methods to ASE-compatible atomistic models, providing a general framework for combining global optimisation, transition state searches, kinetic network analysis, and thermodynamic characterisation with recent developments in machine-learned interatomic potentials.

summary.how: The calculator and socket stay active through the search; kinetic transition networks, mean first-passage times and heat capacities describe vacancy migration.
summary.impact: Low relevance; a defect-kinetics method for Ga2O3, though it shows an ASE-to-MLIP workflow pattern.
summary.what: A persistent socket interface connects the GMIN, OPTIM and PATHSAMPLE energy-landscape tools to ASE-compatible potentials, applied to Ga vacancies in β-Ga2O3 with two NequIP-based potentials.
summary.why: Energy landscape exploration needs many energy and force evaluations, so efficient access to MLIPs is a practical challenge.

title: Exploring Energy Landscapes for Functional Materials: Ga vacancies in $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$

abstract: First-principles calculations implicitly encode bonding and charge transfer, but converting periodic electronic structure into interpretable and transferable descriptors remains challenging. Recently, we introduced Crystal Orbital Guided Iteration To atomic-Orbitals (COGITO), a tool for mapping plane-wave DFT back to an interpretable, minimal basis of adaptive atomic orbitals. Here, we show how the high-dimensional bonding information from COGITO can be reduced into chemically useful descriptors of covalent bonding, charge transfer, and crystal-dependent atomic chemistry without collapsing the real-space origin of the interactions. Compared to methods that use static or orthogonal orbital bases, COGITO descriptors of short- and long-range bonding show more stability and a better ability to distinguish between ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding regimes. Lastly, COGITO reliably decomposes band dispersion into range-resolved contributions, allowing us to verify and add to the orbital origins of silicon's low-symmetry conduction band minimum. Overall, the adaptive COGITO-based descriptors encode electronic structure, offering a well-structured route to expose the orbital interactions and charge transfer responsible for electronic properties.

summary.how: Reduces the high-dimensional COGITO bonding information into descriptors of covalent bonding and charge transfer and decomposes band dispersion into range-resolved parts (silicon conduction band minimum as example).
summary.impact: Low relevance; possible use as interpretable features for MLIP latent-space or bonding analysis, but no thermal transport content.
summary.what: Builds interpretable bonding and charge-transfer descriptors from COGITO, which maps plane-wave DFT onto a minimal basis of adaptive atomic orbitals.
summary.why: Converting periodic electronic structure into interpretable, transferable descriptors remains challenging.

title: Adaptive nonorthogonal atomic orbitals refine charge transfer and bonding descriptors

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) show promise for predicting materials properties, but interpretability remains a challenge, particularly understanding whether attributed feature importance reflects physical reality or statistical artifacts. Here, we present a methods validation study that deliberately overfits a physics-aware GNN ensemble to probe the robustness of feature-ranking approaches. Using the CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy system with three stoichiometries, we train GNNs to predict decomposition enthalpies from DFT-calculated structures while explicitly constraining output weights to encode feature importance. By design, our dataset is limited (approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways) to control compositional complexity and enable precise interrogation of local chemistry effects. We validate that feature rankings capture meaningful local-environment information through a series of atomic swap perturbations: perturbing individual atomic sites and re-ranking features reveals spatial decay consistent with the GNN's interaction cutoff, confirming that weights encode neighbor-shell effects rather than global stoichiometric artifacts alone. Results demonstrate that feature attribution methods can remain physically interpretable even under overfitting, provided validation is rigorous. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy interpretability in materials GNNs and sets the stage for scaling to multiple chemistries and testing generalization across compositional spaces.

summary.how: About 900 binary and 4,500 ternary DFT decomposition pathways; perturbing single sites shows spatial decay consistent with the GNN interaction cutoff.
summary.impact: Relevant to the interest in MLIP and GNN interpretability, with a perturbation-based test that could be adapted to MLIPs. Moderate relevance; different material system.
summary.what: Validates feature attribution in a physics-aware GNN ensemble, deliberately overfit on CoMoFeNiCu decomposition enthalpies, using atomic-swap perturbations.
summary.why: It is unclear whether GNN feature importance reflects physical reality or statistical artifacts.

title: Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy

abstract: Predicting plastic flow in body-centered cubic metals across temperature and strain-rate regimes requires distinguishing structural resistance from kinetic contributions. Here, we develop a temperature dependent mobility law for screw dislocation, integrating thermal activation theory and relativistic effects. Through discrete dislocation dynamics simulations, uniaxial tension and compression simulations were conducted on configurations with different initial dislocation densities, elucidating the correlation between plastic strain rate and key parameters such as stress, temperature, and dislocation density. Subsequently, a unified constitutive model incorporating temperature and strain rate is derived based on microscopic mechanisms. The model naturally bridges microscopic mechanisms to continuum response, resolving the additivity dilemma by establishing explicit physical criteria for how structural resistances and competing kinetic mechanisms superimpose. Through rigorous bottom-up simulations, we quantitatively capture the crossover point where phonon drag overtakes thermal activation, providing a mechanism-based explanation of anomalous thermal hardening. This work enables physically consistent predictions of strength and creep behavior across broad temperature and strain-rate regimes, advancing beyond phenomenological descriptions toward transparent, mechanism-based alloy design.

summary.how: Discrete dislocation dynamics tension and compression simulations at different dislocation densities; identifies the crossover where phonon drag overtakes thermal activation.
summary.impact: Low relevance; dislocation mechanics, with only a loose link to the dislocation-core phonon work (BaTiO3, GaN).
summary.what: Develops a temperature-dependent screw dislocation mobility law and a unified constitutive model for BCC metals from discrete dislocation dynamics.
summary.why: Predicting plastic flow across temperature and strain rates requires separating structural resistance from kinetic contributions.

title: Unified constitutive model of body-centered cubic metals informed by discrete dislocation dynamics

abstract: Abstract Recent experiments on nanoclusters of silver (Ag) embedded in a gold (Au) matrix reveal a substantial enhancement of both the residual resistivity and the coefficient of the linear-in-$T$ thermal resistivity with increasing Ag volume fraction. Since bulk Au and Ag are both weakly coupled electron-phonon systems, these observations raise the possibility of an enhanced effective electron-phonon coupling at the Ag-Au interface. In this work, we explore the consequences of such an enhancement for electronic transport in a strongly inhomogeneous system. An important task is to elucidate the origin of the large interfacial coupling via {\it ab initio} calculation. In this paper, we {\it assume} the presence of such a coupling, and focus on its consequences for residual resistivity and finite temperature scattering in this strongly inhomogeneous scenario. To establish the qualitative physics we construct nanocluster configurations for varying $f$ in a two dimensional geometry, and define a Holstein model on it with weak coupling on the `interior' sites and a strong coupling on the interfacial sites. The model is solved through exact diagonalisation based Langevin dynamics. Our calculations reproduce the qualitative trends of the experimentally observed resistivity enhancement, with its magnitude depending on the choice of interfacial coupling. More importantly, we find that interfacial scattering is strongly spatially differentiated, with the zero temperature and thermal scattering arising from different parts of the interface. We confirm the resistivity trends in three dimensions as well through computation at select parameter points.

summary.how: To establish the qualitative physics we construct nanocluster configurations for varying $f$ in a two dimensional geometry, and define a Holstein model on it with weak coupling on the `interior' sites and a strong coupling on the interfacial sites.
summary.impact: Background reading for First principles, lattice dynamics & thermal MD.
summary.what: More importantly, we find that interfacial scattering is strongly spatially differentiated, with the zero temperature and thermal scattering arising from different parts of the interface.
summary.why: An important task is to elucidate the origin of the large interfacial coupling via {\it ab initio} calculation.

title: Enormous enhancement of resistivity in a nanostructured electron-phonon system

abstract: Atomistic foundation models have emerged as a promising route to DFT-level accuracy for materials simulation with complex chemical environments. However, their reliability across competing bonding regimes and, more importantly, how complex bonding affects predictions of material properties remain unclear. Among materials with competing bonding regimes, sodium storage in hard carbon poses a substantial challenge. Hard carbon features diverse local structural motifs, including defective and curved graphitic regions, amorphous regions, and closed/open pores. Motivated by its importance for Na-ion batteries, we systematically evaluate existing pretrained foundation models based on the MACE architecture across different local Na/C motifs. We find that the pretrained models fail to accurately capture Na-Na and Na-C interactions for metallic Na clusters on graphene. To recover a DFT-level energetic description, we employ targeted fine-tuning, showing that it can describe the energetic stability of local motifs and achieve sufficient transferability to unseen Na/C environments. With the developed fine-tuned model, we establish a correlation between closed-pore radius in hard carbon and plateau voltage, showing that the small pores contribute at larger voltages than large ones, suggesting thus how the developed fine-tuned foundation model can link atomistic information with materials design for complex bonding environments.

summary.how: The pretrained models fail for Na-Na and Na-C interactions in metallic Na clusters on graphene; targeted fine-tuning gives transferability to unseen Na/C environments and links closed-pore radius to plateau voltage.
summary.impact: Relevant as a case of foundation-model failure and fine-tuning with MACE, informing the MACE vs Deep Potential comparison for InGaAs. Moderate relevance; application domain is batteries.
summary.what: Evaluates pretrained MACE-based foundation models on Na/C motifs in hard carbon and fine-tunes them to recover a DFT-level description.
summary.why: Reliability of foundation models across competing bonding regimes is unclear; relevant for Na-ion batteries.

title: Fine-tuned atomistic foundation model for accurate sodium-carbon chemistry in Na-ion batteries

abstract: The intrinsic thermal conductivity ($κ$) of graphene remains highly controversial because of physical and metrological complexities. Although the thermal bridge method enables reliable measurements, sample fabrication remains challenging. Here, we develop a highly efficient patterning and transfer technique to systematically fabricate and characterize suspended bilayer graphene (BLG) thermal bridges with lengths of 1-30 $μ$m. Suspended BLG with unavoidable polymer residues exhibits length-independent thermal conductivity of approximately 570 W/(m K) at room temperature, remaining nearly constant from 250 to 350 K and robust to rigorous surface cleaning and amorphous silicon nitride substrates. Homogeneous non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (HNEMD) simulations show that amorphous carbon coverage of only approximately 0.01 monolayer is sufficient to suppress out-of-plane flexural acoustic (ZA) phonons. These findings challenge the prevailing view that rigid substrates suppress ZA phonons more strongly than surface contamination and identify a robust lower bound of $κ$ governed by amorphous surface scattering. This lower bound reflects heat conduction in graphene under realistic device conditions and provides a reference for fundamental phonon transport studies and the integration of graphene into thermal management applications in electronic devices and chips.

summary.how: A patterning and transfer technique for thermal-bridge devices, measured from 250 to 350 K, plus homogeneous non-equilibrium MD simulations.
summary.impact: Related to interfacial and surface scattering of phonons (GaN/Al2O3 interfaces, grain boundaries); the ZA-suppression argument is a mechanism analogy. Low to moderate relevance.
summary.what: Fabricated suspended bilayer graphene thermal bridges (1 to 30 μm) and measured length-independent κ of about 570 W/m·K at room temperature; HNEMD shows about 0.01 monolayer of amorphous carbon suppresses ZA phonons.
summary.why: The intrinsic thermal conductivity of graphene remains controversial; the work seeks a lower bound under realistic contamination.

title: Lower Bound of Thermal Conductivity in Graphene

abstract: Predicting metastable states with universal machine-learned interatomic potentials requires that they preserve the minima and saddles of the reference potential-energy surface. Here we identify local topology hallucination, in which distinct model minima relax into the same reference basin. This failure arises from mode-selective curvature-sign errors shared by MACE, CHGNet and M3GNet. Curvature signs predicted by two of the three models agreed with density-functional calculations in 55 of 57 positive but only 5 of 56 negative cases. In LiGe$_2$S, two MACE minima connected by a verified saddle relaxed into one density-functional basin. Reference relaxation likewise returned nine of ten selected model minima to their reference basins. A directional test with two displaced reference calculations rejected 9 of 12 prospectively tested model instabilities. Model agreement alone therefore cannot establish that predicted minima are distinct metastable states.

summary.how: Curvature signs from two of three models agreed with DFT in 55 of 57 positive but only 5 of 56 negative cases; a directional two-displacement DFT test rejected 9 of 12 predicted instabilities.
summary.impact: Directly relevant to MLIP failure modes in the MACE-based InGaAs/AlGaN/BAs work: spurious soft or unstable modes would corrupt lattice dynamics and phonon calculations in MLPhonon. Worth reading and adding a DFT check on imaginary modes.
summary.what: Identifies local topology hallucination in universal MLIPs: distinct model minima relax into the same DFT basin, due to curvature-sign errors shared by MACE, CHGNet and M3GNet.
summary.why: Predicting metastable states needs MLIPs to preserve the minima and saddles of the reference potential-energy surface.

title: Local topology hallucinations in universal machine-learned interatomic potentials

abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer near–ab initio accuracy at a fraction of the cost of conventional electronic structure calculations, but their reliability depends critically on the quality and diversity of training data. Here, we present a classical-to-density functional theory (DFT) multi-fidelity workflow for efficient dataset generation, in which long classical molecular dynamics trajectories are supplemented with selectively DFT-optimized configurations to train neural network potentials. We demonstrate this approach on four systems: bulk water, water at the air–water interface, CaSO4 in bulk water, and CaSO4 at the interface. In all cases, the trained models faithfully reproduce reference DFT properties, validating the workflow across both simple and chemically complex environments. We further probe the extrapolation capabilities of the models, showing that bulk-trained networks can generalize to different temperatures, pressures, and interfacial geometries when datasets include targeted augmented configurations. This multi-fidelity strategy thus enables accurate and transferable MLIPs for complex solvated and interfacial systems, bridging the gap between computational efficiency and first-principles accuracy.

summary.how: Tested on bulk water, the air-water interface, and CaSO4 in bulk water and at the interface; also tests extrapolation to other temperatures, pressures and interfacial geometries.
summary.impact: The data-efficiency idea (cheap classical sampling plus targeted DFT) could transfer to the AlGaN or BAs active-learning pipelines, but the systems are aqueous. Low to moderate relevance.
summary.what: A classical-to-DFT multi-fidelity workflow for generating MLIP training data, in which long classical MD trajectories are supplemented with selectively DFT-optimized configurations.
summary.why: MLIP reliability depends on the quality and diversity of the training data, which is costly to produce with DFT.

title: Classical-to-DFT multi-fidelity approach for developing machine learning potentials of aqueous systems

abstract: ABSTRACT Thermal management materials face a persistent challenge: high thermal conductivity ( κ ) and low Young's modulus (E) are often mutually exclusive. Stiff materials typically conduct heat well while compliant materials tend to thermally insulate. Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) offer exceptional structural tunability that breaks this trade‐off, yet a systematic understanding of κ ‐E decoupling remains elusive. Here we establish an interpretable machine learning framework integrating molecular simulations, six benchmarked models, and SHAP‐based feature analysis to screen over 52 000 topologically valid three‐dimensional COFs. Using random forest as the optimal model, we identify 26 COFs that simultaneously achieve high κ (> 0.8 W m − 1 K − 1 ) and low E (< 8 GPa), a combination difficult to attain by conventional design. SHAP analysis reveals that decoupling arises from nonlinear cooperative actions of multiple descriptors rather than single‐feature tuning. Phonon‐level transport analyses show that intermediate density, strong covalent connectivity, moderate porosity, and low linker fragment complexity balance volumetric heat capacity, phonon group velocity, and phonon lifetime, enabling high κ while preserving low E. This work provides a blueprint for thermally conductive yet mechanically compliant COFs and establishes a generalizable workflow for exploring property decoupling in framework materials.

summary.how: Molecular simulations, six benchmarked ML models (random forest best), SHAP feature analysis and phonon-level transport analysis.
summary.impact: Low relevance to the listed projects (organic frameworks), but the SHAP-plus-phonon-analysis workflow is a transferable idea for interpretable ML on κ.
summary.what: Interpretable ML framework screens over 52,000 3D covalent organic frameworks and identifies 26 with κ above 0.8 W/m·K and Young's modulus below 8 GPa.
summary.why: High thermal conductivity and low stiffness are normally mutually exclusive in thermal management materials.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning Reveals Design Rules for Thermal‐Mechanical Decoupling in Covalent Organic Frameworks

abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) now approach density functional theory (DFT) accuracy at a fraction of its cost, but the practical benefit is limited by software fragmentation: each state-of-the-art architecture is released as a separate codebase, with its own data format, configuration system, training loop and molecular-dynamics interface. Comparing two architectures on the same dataset, or moving a trained model into a production simulation, therefore requires substantial re-engineering. We introduce IANN (InterAtomic Neural Network), an open-source PyTorch framework that reimplements equivariant graph neural networks - PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA - behind a unified data object, a unified trainer and a single deployment route, so that the architecture is a one-word change in a configuration dictionary. Forces, stresses and virials are obtained for every architecture from one analytic differentiation of the energy with respect to the edge vectors of the atomic graph, exact under periodic boundary conditions. Distributed training is configured automatically from the SLURM, PBS or MPI environment, so the same script runs unchanged from a workstation to a multi-node GPU allocation. Self-describing checkpoints serve directly as ASE calculators, as ensembles reporting uncertainties, or as TorchScript models run inside LAMMPS through bundled C++ pair styles with single- and multi-GPU inference. Trained on a common dataset of millions of structures, the architectures can be compared under identical conditions. We further release PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures from MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN and MatPESr2SCAN, spanning the PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN…

summary.how: Forces and stresses come from one analytic differentiation w.r.t. edge vectors; automatic distributed training under SLURM/PBS/MPI; checkpoints work as ASE calculators, ensembles, or TorchScript models in LAMMPS via C++ pair styles with multi-GPU inference.
summary.impact: Useful for the InGaAs (DeePMD vs MACE) and AlGaN MLIP pipelines and MLPhonon: one framework to compare architectures on the same data and deploy into LAMMPS. Worth testing.
summary.what: Introduces IANN, an open-source PyTorch framework reimplementing PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2/V3 and UMA behind one data object, trainer and deployment route; also releases PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million DFT structures.
summary.why: Software fragmentation makes comparing MLIP architectures or moving a trained model into production simulations require heavy re-engineering.

title: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation

abstract: The thermal conductivities of (001) $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films deposited on $c$-plane sapphire substrates were measured with frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR). The thermal conductivity increases from 1.83 $^{+0.19}_{-0.18}$ W/m$\cdot$K to 2.26 $^{+0.35}_{-0.40}$ W/m$\cdot$K as the thicknesses increase from 159 nm to 689 nm. This weak thickness dependence indicates that the majority of the intrinsic phonon mean free paths are smaller than the range of investigated film thicknesses. First-principles-based calculations that include phonon-phonon and phonon-boundary scattering capture this size-dependent behavior and support our experimental observation. Temperature-dependent measurements of a 689 nm film from 293 to 400 K show a decrease in thermal conductivity with increasing temperature due to enhanced phonon-phonon scattering. A weaker temperature dependence is observed in a 159 nm film where phonon-boundary scattering becomes more prominent. At comparable film thicknesses, our measured $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ films exhibit lower values of cross-plane thermal conductivity than the other experimentally measured Ga$_2$O$_3$ polymorphs. Our experimental observations are supported by prior predictions, which suggest that the low thermal conductivity of $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ results from its complex crystal structure, which leads to increased anharmonicity and lower phonon group velocities relative to other polymorphs. Thermal management strategies, such as integration with high-thermal-conductivity substrates, may thus be required to mitigate self-heating for $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$-based electronic devices.

summary.how: Frequency-domain thermoreflectance (293 to 400 K) combined with first-principles calculations including phonon-phonon and phonon-boundary scattering.
summary.impact: Relevant to the GaN/AlGaN HEMT and GaN/Al2O3 interface projects: a template for size-dependent κ with first-principles BTE and an FDTR benchmark for wide-bandgap films (McGaughey group, a watched author). Moderate relevance.
summary.what: Measured cross-plane thermal conductivity of (001) κ-Ga2O3 thin films on sapphire by FDTR: 1.83 to 2.26 W/m·K for 159 to 689 nm thickness.
summary.why: To understand thermal limits and self-heating of κ-Ga2O3 electronics, whose thermal conductivity is lower than other Ga2O3 polymorphs.

title: Low cross-plane thermal conductivity of $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films
